anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > The centre of gravity: "To balance the broom, you must move the support closer to the brush head."
purpose: Illustrate qualitatively how an object's centre of gravity shifts away from the geometric midpoint toward the region of greater mass concentration using an uneven broom.
what_to_show: Two comparative broom diagrams on a white background. Left diagram: a broom supported at its geometric midpoint by a triangular pivot; the heavy brush head on the right tips downward with a curved green arrow and label 'tips down'. Right diagram: the same broom supported near the brush head by a triangular pivot; the broom rests balanced horizontally. Annotations state 'Balance point follows mass concentration' and 'More mass in brush -> balance point shifts toward it'.
what_to_notice: The outline of the broom has a geometric middle, but the balance point shifts toward the heavy brush head where mass is concentrated.

anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > The centre of gravity: "We replace all the distributed gravitational pulls with one equivalent downward force."
purpose: Show how distributed gravitational pulls acting on every small mass element throughout an extended irregular body are mathematically modelled as a single equivalent weight vector acting vertically downward through its centre of gravity.
what_to_show: A two-panel model comparison diagram. Left panel shows an irregular grey object with six downward vertical grey arrows distributed across the shape labelled 'many small pulls'. A horizontal green arrow labelled 'model as' points to the right panel. Right panel shows the same irregular shape with a single central solid black dot labelled 'centre of gravity' and a single downward vertical green vector arrow labelled 'W' and 'one weight force'. Explanatory note states 'W is weight. Its arrow is vertical and downward'.
what_to_notice: Physicists do not track thousands of tiny gravitational pulls separately. The distributed weight is replaced by a single downward force W acting through the centre of gravity.

anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > The centre of gravity: "Its centre of gravity shifts away from the geometric midpoint toward the region of greater mass concentration."
purpose: Provide authentic past-paper evidence showing how Cambridge examiners assess non-uniform objects where the centre of gravity does not coincide with the geometric midpoint.
what_to_show: Authentic examination figure from Cambridge paper 9702/21/M/J/17 Question 3 Fig. 3.1 showing a horizontal 50 cm non-uniform bar AB supported on a triangular pivot P at 12 cm from end B, with its weight 0.25 N acting downward at its centre of gravity 20 cm from end B (8 cm left of P), suspended cylinder of weight 0.60 N at end A, and load X at end B.
what_to_notice: Notice that the bar's weight arrow is placed at its centre of gravity (20 cm from end B), which is distinct from both the pivot P (12 cm from B) and the geometric midpoint (25 cm from B). In moment calculations, the relevant distance is the 8 cm between pivot P and the centre of gravity.

anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > Turning effects and the pivot: "We write this perpendicular distance as $d_\perp$."
purpose: Define the geometrical relationship between a pivot, the line of action of an applied force, and the perpendicular distance d_perp, showing the resulting clockwise turning tendency.
what_to_show: A circular pivot P on the left connected to a horizontal handle extending rightward. At the right end, a vertical downward force arrow labelled 'force F' is applied. A vertical dashed line extends upward and downward through the force arrow labelled 'line of action'. A horizontal dimension line at the bottom extends from pivot P to the line of action, meeting at a square right-angle symbol (90 degrees) and labelled 'd_perp'. A curved green arrow near pivot P indicates 'clockwise tendency'.
what_to_notice: The perpendicular distance d_perp is measured from the pivot to the extended line of action at a right angle (90 degrees), not along an arbitrary slant.

anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > Perpendicular distance for angled bodies and forces: "The perpendicular distance from the pivot to this vertical line is the horizontal base of the right-angled triangle."
purpose: Demonstrate the geometric resolution required to find the perpendicular distance from a pivot to the vertical line of action of an object's weight when the body is inclined at an angle.
what_to_show: A vertical wall on the left with hatch marks supporting a hinge H. A rectangular sign rises from H at 30 degrees above the horizontal. The centre of gravity G is marked with a solid dot 0.60 m along the sign. A vertical downward arrow from G represents weight 'W = 49.05 N'. A horizontal dashed line extends from H to the vertical line of action of W, meeting at a 90-degree right-angle marker and labelled 'd_perp approx 0.520 m'. Angle arc at H is labelled '30 deg'. Annotation states 'Shortest distance to a vertical line is horizontal'.
what_to_notice: Because weight acts vertically downward, the shortest distance from the hinge to its line of action is strictly horizontal. The slanted 0.60 m length must be multiplied by cos 30 degrees to obtain the horizontal perpendicular distance d_perp.

anchor: Centre of gravity and the moment of a force > The turning effect of an object's weight: "Therefore, the perpendicular distance for a weight force is the horizontal separation between the pivot and the centre of gravity."
purpose: Provide authentic examiner apparatus evidence showing a pivoted beam balance where an added weight produces a moment about the pivot.
what_to_show: Authentic examination apparatus figure from Cambridge paper 9702/23/M/J/21 Question 3 Fig. 3.1 showing a rigid rod pivoted about a point, with a spring attached 1.8 cm right of the pivot, a pan with centre 6.2 cm right of the pivot, and a 52.6 cm pointer to the left indicating on a vertical millimetre scale.
what_to_notice: An object placed on the pan has its weight acting vertically downward through the centre of the pan. Its moment about the pivot is found by multiplying its weight mg by the horizontal perpendicular distance of 6.2 cm (6.2 x 10^-2 m).
